pages.lede: Plumbing has three occupational constants: your knees are on hard floors half the day, water finds you eventually, and much of the work happens in a customer's home where you are the company's entire impression. The kit list answers all three.

blocks.h2: Wet work and waste work are different problems
blocks.html:
Clean-side wet — a pressurised joint letting go, a full trap — is a comfort problem: quick-dry synthetics and a spare top in the van solve what cotton would turn into a cold afternoon. Waste-side work is a hygiene problem: disposable nitrile over-gloves, sleeves that push clear, and a wash-up kit in the van are the professional baseline, and anything soaked on a waste job gets bagged for the wash, not worn to the next customer's kitchen.

The knee story is the one to take seriously: plumbing is a lifetime of kneeling on tile, and EN 14404 trousers with pads actually fitted — plus a kneeling mat for long jobs — is the cheapest pension contribution in the trade. Gas-registered work adds its own FR-adjacent rules near heat; the heat glove guide covers soldering-adjacent hands.

items.l: The soaked-shirt job always precedes the customer meeting
Waste-side clothing travels sealed, washes hot, separately
A named, branded chest is worth a review star on its own

faq.a: Holster-pocket work trousers with EN 14404 knee-pad pockets — fittings and fixings ride in the holsters, and the pads handle a trade that kneels on tile half the day. Stretch fabrics help in tight cupboard work.
A toe cap earns its place — radiators, baths and boilers are exactly the dropped-heavy-object risk S-codes exist for. S1P covers indoor domestic work; S3 suits first-fix sites and anything outdoors.

faq.q: What should plumbers wear in customers' homes?
faq.a: Clean embroidered kit, overshoes or unlaced-friendly boots at the door, and dust sheets down — presentation is repeat-business economics in domestic trades. A spare dry top in the van keeps the standard up after wet jobs.

pages.lede: Carpentry kit is a dexterity negotiation: the trade needs fingertips free enough for a pencil line and protected enough for a splinter-rich, blade-adjacent day — while the dust the work makes is more dangerous than most of the tools making it.

heroMeta.l: Hardwood dust is not a nuisance dust

Spec

blocks.h2: The sander is more dangerous than the saw
blocks.html:
Cuts announce themselves; dust doesn't. Hardwood dust is a recognised carcinogen and MDF dust carries its binder resins — which is why the mask rule for carpentry isn't the nuisance-dust FFP1 in the multipack but FFP2 for softwood work and FFP3 for hardwood and MDF, worn fitted, with extraction doing the heavy lifting on machines. A bearded joiner needs the fit conversation, not a better disposable.

The glove negotiation resolves the same way as the gloves hub argues: a thin coated glove that stays on beats a tough one in a pocket — cut level B–C for sheet-material days, bare-handed only where a specific machine's rules demand it. And the workshop discipline travels with the kit: close cuffs, no drawstrings, crew-neck over hoodie near anything that spins.

items.l: Scratched, fogged glasses end up in pockets — coatings keep them on faces
Keep FFP2s and FFP3s both in the van, labelled — grade to the board
S1P lives in the workshop; S3 goes to first fix — two pairs beat one compromise

faq.q: What mask do carpenters need for MDF?
faq.a: FFP3 — MDF dust combines fine hardwood-like particles with binder resins, putting it in the top disposable grade alongside hardwood dust. Softwood hand-tool work sits at FFP2. Extraction at the machine remains the primary control; the mask is the backstop.

For handling, carrying and sheet work, yes — thin coated gloves at cut level B–C keep splinters and board edges out without killing feel. At specific rotating machinery, follow the machine's rules; some operations are safer bare-handed than with a snaggable glove.

Holster-pocket work trousers are the trade favourite — fixings and small tools at hand height — with EN 14404 knee-pad pockets earning their place for second fix and flooring work. Stretch fabric helps the up-down rhythm of the job.

pages.metaDesc: Kit for bricklayers — abrasion-4 gloves against block texture, cement-burn awareness, knee protection for kerb and DPC courses, and layers for the most exposed trade on site.
pages.lede: Brickwork grinds kit down like no other trade: block texture eats gloves, mortar eats skin, and the scaffold is the most weather-exposed workplace on site. The list below is chosen for attrition.

heroMeta.l: Block texture sets the glove spec

Spec
Why

blocks.h2: Cement burns don't hurt until they're deep
blocks.html:
Wet mortar is strongly alkaline, and its burns are insidious: prolonged skin contact — mortar in a glove, kneeling in fresh muck, a boot full of it — causes chemical burns that don't sting until the damage is done. The kit answers: gloves that keep mortar out (gauntlet cuffs for mixing), waterproof knee protection on fresh-mortar work rather than trousers soaking through, rinsing splashes off skin promptly, and never finishing a day in mortar-soaked clothing. It's the trade's version of the wet-concrete rule.

The other constant is silica: dry-cutting brick, block and stone is FFP3-and-extraction territory, no exceptions — the FFP guide carries the warning in full.

items.l: Abrasion-4 coated gloves are consumables on blockwork — budget accordingly
Cement dermatitis ends careers; the cream-and-wash routine is protective kit
Gloves soaked in mortar are a chemical compress — swap them

faq.a: Coated gloves at EN 388 abrasion level 4, bought boxed — block and brick texture destroys lighter gloves in days. For mixing and heavy mortar contact, gauntlet-cuff styles keep the caustic material off wrists and out of the glove.

faq.q: Can wet cement burn your skin?
faq.a: Yes — mortar and concrete are strongly alkaline, and prolonged contact causes chemical burns that develop painlessly. Keep mortar out of gloves and boots, rinse splashes promptly, use waterproof knee protection on fresh work, and never work on in soaked clothing.

faq.q: Do bricklayers need a dust mask?
faq.a: For any dry cutting or chasing of brick, block or stone — yes, FFP3, because masonry dust is respirable crystalline silica. Wet cutting and on-tool extraction are the primary controls; the mask backs them up.

blocks.h2: Wind first, and dress for the harness
blocks.html:
Ground-level layering logic underestimates roofs: wind is the multiplier, stripping heat through fleece that would be fine in the yard. The roof answer is windproofing early — softshell over base layer — with the waterproof shell for actual rain, because roof work in real rain usually stops for the same reason the tiles are slippery.

Harness compatibility quietly shapes the wardrobe: bulky insulated jackets bunch under straps and hide the fit check, so roofers run trim layers under the harness and put warmth in the base and mid layers instead. Torch-on and hot works add the flame layer: an EN 407-rated glove, natural-fibre or FR outer near the torch, and the melt-layer rule from the FR hub applying to whatever's underneath.

items.l: Worn tread on a roof is a different order of problem — inspect like PPE, because it is
Wind turns loose kit into sails and blindfolds — trim fits at height
Roofers burn in April — neck flaps and SPF are summer PPE up there

faq.q: What boots are best for roofing?
faq.a: S3 boots with an aggressive slip-rated sole and a flexible forefoot — grip on wet tile, membrane and crawl boards is the primary spec, and a stiff sole fights the footwork. Tread condition gets inspected like the safety equipment it is.

faq.q: What do roofers wear in winter?
faq.a: Windproofing before insulation: wicking base layer, windproof softshell, and a waterproof shell for real weather — roof wind doubles the effective cold, and bulky coats fight the harness. Warm gloves that still grip, and a helmet-compatible beanie, finish it.

Work at height favours chinstrap-retained climbing-style helmets (EN 12492) that stay on in a fall or gust, and many roofing contractors now specify them over traditional EN 397 lids. The site or employer's rules make the final call — check before buying.

blocks.h2: Sanding and solvents are the serious end
blocks.html:
The romance of the trade is brushwork; the exposure is preparation. Machine-sanding filler and softwood sits at FFP2; MDF and — critically — old painted surfaces step up to FFP3, because pre-modern coatings can carry lead and the dust deserves respect (suspect lead paint has its own safe-work rules beyond a mask). Extraction-equipped sanders do the heavy lifting; the mask backs them up.

Solvent handling sets the glove spec: nitrile resists the white spirits and 2-pack products that swell latex, with a gauntlet-and-SDS approach for anything industrial. And whites earn their second function at day's end: emulsion-marked cotton boil-washes back to white — the whites playbook transfers almost intact.

items.l: A splash you see on your thigh is a splash that missed the carpet — barely
Disposable nitrile for coatings; a coated pair for prep and ladders
Finished-floor-friendly footwear is part of the professional impression

faq.q: Why do painters and decorators wear white?
faq.a: Function dressed as tradition: white shows every splash and smudge instantly — a wearable warning system in customer houses — hides white-paint marks between washes, and boil-washes clean. It also reads as professional in a trade sold on neatness.

faq.q: What mask do decorators need for sanding?
faq.a: FFP2 for filler and softwood; FFP3 for MDF and old painted surfaces — pre-modern paint can carry lead, and suspected lead paint work has safe-working rules beyond mask choice. Extraction sanders remain the primary control.

faq.q: What gloves work with paint and solvents?
faq.a: Nitrile — disposable for coatings work, heavier nitrile gauntlets for solvent-heavy tasks. White spirit and 2-pack products degrade latex quickly; check the product's safety data sheet where anything industrial is involved.
